maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
1.	Two; one at Ottawa and one at Moncton.
2.	The Ottawa station, $18,253.20, and Moncton, $22,500.
3.	Twenty cars have been equipped at a total cost of $10,843.39; average per car, $542.17.
4.	Equipment is placed on trains, not for the purpose of entertaining the staff, but to afford information and entertainment for passengers, and thereby attract passenger business to Canadian National lines.
5 and 6. No direct revenue, but the management have ample proof, based upon reports from the Traffic department, that the advertising obtained by the aid of these stations has resulted in increased earnings for the railways. During the month of January, 1925, ten programmes were broadcasted from the Ottawa station. The management received 3,122 telegrams, cards and letters acknowledging the broadcasts, or an average of 312 per concert. The acknowledgments were received from all sections of Canada, practically the entire United States, and Cuba.
The average number of communications received from the station at Moncton is 350. Those are received from the Maritime provinces, Newfoundland, New England states, Quebec and Ontario. In one mail recently, there were received at Moncton fourteen letters from the British Isles acknowledging receipt of the Moncton broadcast, and it is fair to assume that the interest displayed by the recipients of Canadian National Railway broadcasts will result in increased business to the railway.

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: GRAVES OF CANADIAN SOLDIERS IN FRANCE
speechtext:
1.	Has the attention of the government been called to the action of the French government in proposing to remove the bodies of two hundred Canadian soldiers buried in the Canadian cemetery at Lieven, near Loos, in France ?
2.	Is this action not in direct violation of the agreement in existence that no cemetery containing more than forty bodies will be moved, as this cemetery was carefully selected, and what action has been taken by the Government, or the Canadian and British War Graves Commission, to regulate these matters?
3.	Has the Canadian government any check in the matter, and are they aware of these removals before they take place, and is the Canadian government consulted in the matter, and what action has or will be taken?

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: GRAVES OF CANADIAN SOLDIERS IN FRANCE
speechtext:
1.	It is presumed that the question refers to Corkscrew British cemetery which contains the graves of some 200 soldiers of whom however only 36 are Canadians.
2.	The government is unaware of any such agreement. The permanent establishment of cemeteries is subject to the French law of hygiene and the consent of communal authorities. There has however always been an understanding that cemeteries containing less than forty bodies must be moved.
3.	Under agreements with the French and Belgian governments the Imperial War Graves Commission, on which Canada has her own representative, is qualified to act in these matter's. Very few removals have been necessary and these have been made only in cases in which the sites for uncontrollable reasons have become definitely unsuitable. In the case in question it is understood that the burials were originally made among the coal mines and that the site is surrounded by railway lines. It became apparent that the graves could not be preserved in proper permanent honour in the original situation. The French authorities have insisted on removal and have refused in this instance to

give to the commission a perpetual concession of the site. The new location is in Loos British cemetery which is being made into a very beautiful cemetery where the bodies will rest in peaceful and dignified surroundings. Notification of such removals is given by the commission to relatives direct.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a revision of the rules is desirable, and that for this purpose a special committee should be appointed to consider and report upon such revision at this session.
He said: In rising to speak to this resolution may I assure the House that I am in agreement with what I take to be the general consensus of opinion, that in the main the rules and practices of parliament achieve the ends for which they were instituted. Coming to us as they do as the wisdom of long experience, they provide in some way or other for almost every contingency which might conceivably arise in the conduct of public business. Amongst other things they ensure a free discussion; they make for despatch and efficiency in matters of business; they ensure against snap verdicts; and in a very comprehensive way regulate the deliberations o|f parliament with a degree of speed, efficiency, fairness and harmony which is on the whole very satisfactory. But, in thus paying what I trust is due respect to parliamentary rules, I am not prepared to admit the improbability of improvement. By the very nature of the British constitution which we follow in our Canadian parliament, current necessities are the parents of precedents, and there are times when even parliamentary rules are more honoured in the breach than in the observance. I will give at a later stage of my argument some of these instances in which parliamentary rules seem to work against the best interests of parliament. If it be admitted that there is even a possibility of improving to any extent any rule of parliament, then I contend that the means of making such an improvement should be provided for by the appointment of a committee, such as is proposed in this resolution. In recent years the desirability of revising the rules of parliament and in even going so far as to renovate the whole machinery of government has been apparent both in Canada and Great Britain. The British government in 1917 appointed a committee under the chairmanship of Lord Haldane, which included within the scope of its reference the question of revision of parliamentary rules. It is true the inquiry undertaken by Lord Haldane's committee was very much more comprehensive than is suggested in this resolution, covering as it did the whole governmental institution in all its phases. The reference to that committee was as follows:

Rules of the House
To inquire into the responsibllitiea of the various departments of central executives, and to advise in what manner the exercise and distribution by the government of its functions should be improved.
That parliamentary practice and rules were included in this reference is proved by the fact that in a section of the report of that committee under the heading of Parliamentary Control, recommendations are made regarding alterations in parliamentary practice that would provide for a larger measure of control by parliament, especially in the matter of public expenditure. Then a select committee on procedure of the House in the British parliament in its ninth annual report in 1918 recommended radical departures from present practices, especially in dealing with the estimates in comlmittee of the Whole; but these are not the only instances where inquiries have been made with a view to revising parliamentary rules and procedure. I would draw the attention of the House to the Murray report on the reorganization of the public service of Canada which was made in 1912. This also includes a rather severe criticism of parliamentary practice in some very important particulars. Then in 1919 our Senate appointed a special committee to consider and report on the "possibility of bettering the machinery of government". The scope of that reference, it will be seen also, was very much wider than I am proposing in this resolution, but nevertheless it also includes what I am asking, namely; a consideration of the question of a revision of the rules. The committee of the Senate made use of the report of Lord Haldane's committee of the Murray report, and also made reference to the select standing committee of the British house to which I have referred, and seems to have agreed in the main that the recommendations of these bodies were desirable for Canada. I make reference, Mr. Speaker, to these investigations by committees of the British parliament and of the Canadian Senate to show that the desirability of revising the rules of parliament, is not merely a whim of my own or of some few members of the House.
Not only do these reports that I have mentioned, coming from these committees, indicate the need of modification and alteration in parliamentary practice, but they emphasize the need of improvement in matters much more fundamental. So far, all I think will be prepared to admit that no rules, whether they be parliamentary or any other kind of rules are perfect, so that I will begin by placing my request for a committee on the very lowest basis, which is this, that no rules are perfect, our .parliamentary rules are
not perfect, and that there is at least a possibility of improving them.
The attention which has been given to the whole question of government and parliamentary control by the aforementioned committees tends to show that a revision of the rules is advisable. I desire to point out some examples which, I hope, will appeal to all members of the House, as they are certainly familiar with the practices to which I will draw their attention. In pointing out some rules of parliament that, in my opinion, could stand revision, I do so without attempting to make any distinction whatever between rules and practices of parliament. If there exists any such distinction, I shall have to leave it to some legal mind to show where that distinction lies. So far as I am able to observe, the rules and the practices of parliament both seem to be one as regards the conduct of the House. The present practices of parliament prohibit to a very large degree parliamentary control over public expenditure. I should like, in this connection, to summarize the Murray report. It says that control of parliament over expenditure is negligible; that the theory of control is very complete, but the practice is of little value. Few, it seems to me, will assert that control of parliament over expenditure is anything more than a formality. It is not a real control. We have, of course, full liberty' to criticize expenditures, but we have no control over what they shall be. Mr. Lloyd George, on this question, has something to say which I think is worth quoting. Speaking in the British House of Commons,he says:
I do not think the present methods of parliamentary control are efficient, but that is not a change which has come about through the new administration. I have always thought that the methods of parliamentary control, and I speak here as a fairly old parliamentarian, rather tended to give undue prominence to trivialities-my right hon. friend and I have talked over this matter many a time-and on the other hand that it rather tended to minimise and ignore realities. Whether you can improve upon that I personally have never had any doubt, but I have always thought- I do not know whether I carry anyone with me on this except my hon. friend who sits there-that the French system was a more effective one-the system whereby ministers have to appear before parliamentary committees.
A select committee of the British House framed a questionnaire which they sent out to the leading minds of the nation and they received a reply which would seem to bear out the view of Mr. Lloyd George which I have just quoted. I quote now from the report of that committee:
The replies show, with few exceptions, a consensus of opinion that the present system of parliamentary control over expenditure is inadequate. In that view we concur. Indeed our terms of reference themselves, inviting proposals to render control more effective, in-
Rules oj the Howe

nation was caused when the leader of the Labour party (Mr. Woodsworth) forestalled the leader of the official opposition and moved an amendment to the budget-the only amendment that could be moved. Without debating the advantages which might accrue from a change in that respect, I draw the practice to the attention of the House in the hope that this is another instance where hon. members will agree that a revision might well take place. Surely it will be agreed that the Progressive party, the Labour or any other group has just as good a right as the official opposition to move such an amendment; and I think it will be also generally agreed that the present rule in limiting the amendment in this instance to the official opposition, forbids the fullest expression of opinion.
Then let me take one other illustration, the appointment of committees by the government. The government is always careful to have a large majority of its own supporters on each committee. This practice, of course, arises out of the two-party system, but in my opinion it might very well be dropped. Surely it might be better for the government to leave such committees more or less free from domination, and by so doing it is possible that ideas more favourable to a higher type of legislation might at least be reflected in the recommendations of these committees, even if such recommendations should be killed later by the government party on the floor of the House.
I think I have perhaps drawn the attention of the House to a sufficient number of cases to show the advisability of appointing a committee to inquire into the whole question of the revision of the rules, and I hope that what I have presented in support of my resolution will indicate the nature of the inquiry which I propose. If the House is of the opinion that no change is desirable or possible, then my speech will be at least a protest against its judgment. If, however, it agrees that improvements may be effected in some of our parliamentary practices, this resolution should be adopted and the committee asked for forthwith appointed. Such a committee might not bring immediate results, but by taking this step we would be at least ready to move forward when the proper time came, for the House would be in possession of all the information necessary to deal intelligently with the subject. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that my views will be favourably received by hon. members. No harm can possibly come by a committee of this House going into the question of a revision of the rules. If such a committee should find there is no basis for any alteration, that there is no room for improve-

ment, no harm would be done by the information being placed before the House. I hope, therefore, that this resolution will be adopted and the committee asked for appointed at thi3 session.

speechtext:
I gladly accept the invitation of the Prime Minister to express my views on this question. Ever since I came here I have had a growing conviction that our procedure makes for inefficiency and waste of time in several fairly important respects. I do believe, of course as the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) has so well said, that most of our rules, having been based on long experience, are most excellent; that the worthy objects of freedom of speech, the saving of time, and the prevention of surprises and snap verdicts are very well provided for in the rules as at present existing; but I should like to submit very emphatically to the House that these rules have been built up when conditions were very different from what they are to-day, and very different from what they are likely to be in the near future. We ought to adapt our machinery to existing conditions, and not to conditions that have passed, and the time has arrived now, I think, when a revision of the rules, or at least some of the rules, ought to be undertaken.
Reference has been made to several matters which, in my opinion, are worthy of serious

Rules oj the Home
consideration, and I sincerely hope that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) will join with those of us who are in favour of the resolution in order that he may be prevented in the future from being caught as he was last year. I think we ought to provide the greatest liberty to all the various groups in this House for the expression of their opinions.
There is another reason why the resolution ought to pass, and I wish to bring that before the House very briefly. There are three resolutions on the order paper which refer either to the work of committees in general, or to the rules of the House. They are No. 2, No. 6, and No. 14. No. 2 is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, one full day a week for the whole session should be set aside for private members, on which day notices of motion shall have precedence over other business.
This is a motion which will probably be debated shortly in this House, and it occurs to me that after a preliminary debate here, the subject matter of it might very fittingly be referred to the same committee which, if it is appointed will be charged with the revision of the rules.
No. 6, standing in the name of the hon. member for Maeleod (Mr. Coote), refers to the consideration of the estimates, already referred to by the mover of the resolution before us. This is also a matter of 4 pm. a very similar character and might be more particularly inquired into by the special committee which is being asked for.
No. 14, standing in my name, refers to the size of committees. I have been collecting some information on this point which in due course I propose to submit to the House, and in that case too it seems to me that after a preliminary discussion here the best plan would be to submit the matter to a committee for further investigation.
There are, then, at least three resolutions already on the order paper, in addition to the one now being debated, which might very properly be turned over, after a preliminary discussion in this House, to committees. It would seem to me, then, entirely the part of wisdom that in view of these four different resolutions, which might be all solved in the same way, the government and the official opposition ought to agree with us to have this committee appointed. Let us not be afraid of undertaking a little extra work. Nothing will be done worth while unless we are prepared bo do some work and to put in some time here. It may be very nice for us to come down here and sit for a short time and get home again as quickly as we can, but I sub-27
mat, Mr. Speaker, that the country is going to suffer if that is to be the attitude of hon. members. In that connection I heard a little story the other day which might be worth repeating bo the House. I hope it will not give offence to any hon. member. It is the story of a couple, I do not know just where they lived but at all events they were Canadians, and were notorious for their idleness. A friend asked Joe one day how he and his wife managed to put in the time. "Well," he said "sometimes we sits and thinks; sometimes we just sits." I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall not be guilty of the last practice in this House.
The Prime Minister has already intimated that the government has no objection provided there is a reasonable demand from this House for the appointment of a committee. I have submitted to the House that there are three other resolutions which, after a preliminary discussion in this House, which will come I dare say in the near future, might be very properly turned over for further inquiry to that same committee. It seems to me, then, that there is every reason why this demand should be acceded to and why the resolution should be passed, and no good reason that has been advanced, at all events so far why the request should not -be granted; and I hope that in further response to the Prime Minister's invitation a number of members in various parts of the House will express their views.

I
notice that we have 120 rules in this House, and that the British parliament gets along with 95 rules. I think it is just as well that we do n-ot. have too many rules, or rules too binding. That may enable us at times to get over difficulties in regard to procedure. I would not be in favour of having rules invariably strict and binding covering all the proceedings that take place in this House, because that might hamper freedom of speech, and restrain members from taking action that would really be in the interest of the whole country. We want to have the rules of the House broad enough and wide enough to make for the efficient conduct of our business, ratheT than to restrict the members to rigid rules. While it is no doubt absolutely necessary that we should have rules to guide our procedure in this House, it is undoubtedly true that the rules have a sort of stifling effect upon new members and often prevent them taking action. Many a time they might feel it in the interests of their constituents to speak, but they do not do so just because they are afraid they are not sufficiently well acquainted with the rules of the House.



Rules oj the House
Two years ago the leader of the Progressives, then the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) moved an amendment to the amendment to the budget which was ruled out of order. I think it was very desirable that such a thing should have been allowed, if it was deemed necessary to do it. The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) also referred to the methods followed in criticising the estimates. I do not know whether any rule to improve the present method can be adopted, but I am prepared to say that those now in vogue are very unsatisfactory. I cannot but feel that very often the whole procedure is something in] the nature of a farce. It cannot be argued that we do criticise the estimates in any intelligent manner, and I should like to see some improvement inaugurated which would bring about better results.
There is another custom that I should like to see changed and that is the practice under which the government feels bound to look upon it as a motion of want of confidence if any recommendation they bring forward is voted down by the House. I think that practice has a stifling effect upon hon. members on their own side, and that it is possible to have a free expression of opinion, and even an untrammelled vote, without it being construed in any such manner. It is quite a common thing, even upon some very trifling matter to hear the assertion, "If this is rejected we will have to go to the country." As if going to the country were a very trifling matter. It is a serious thing.

speechtext:
It differs in some respects from the present resolution, but possibly it might be combined with that of my hon. friend (Mr. Irvine). The difference consists in this; that while my hon. friend's resolution seeks to refer the matter to a special committee, I am proposing to have a reference to the select committee on Standing Orders. That is the committee, I understand, that is presided over by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin). We all know that hon. gentleman's thorough grasp of the rules of the House, and it seems unnecessary that another committee should be appointed. There are plenty of committees already, and the hon. member for Shefford very efficiently presides over the selelct standing committee which now is the body appointed to deal with such matters.
My resolution deals with the proposed changes in an entirely different aspect from that of the present motion. I do not ask for, nor do I approve of, what I might call the fundamental changes that he suggests; for example, in proposing to aLlow hon. members in committee of the Whole to move for the increase of a vote. That would produce chaos more or less; it would lead to what is called log-rolling. A section on one side of the House would agree with another section, perhaps on the government side, for an increase of a certain vote. The man on the government side of the House dare not vote against a motion in the interest of his own constituency perhaps, and yet he might be acting contrary to the settled policy of the

Rides oj the House
government. Whatever administration is in power ought to be in control of the finances of the country; otherwise it would practically be impossible to carry on the government. I think it would be a great mistake to do away with that provision.
The hon. member also spoke about the impossibility of having a resolution of a certain character presented because it would be out of order, inasmuch as it would pledge the government to expenditure of public money. That also, of course, is objectionable for the reason that I have already given. Under the change proposed we should find members of the House who bear no responsibility for Canada's finances, voting for untold expenditures. Besides, the difficulty complained of is not so serious as it would appear to be because it can easily be overcome by asking the government to inquire into or take note of a particular situation. So that there is no hindrance in any sense to a full debate in the House on any given subject.
Another suggestion of the hon. member was that we should do away with the government majority on committees. Well, I do not think the leader of the opposition, or any hon. member who has had any experience in the cabinet, would agree to a suggestion of that kind. A government must have some measure of control over a committee corresponding with the control which it exercises in the House.
Now, turning to my own resolution I propose to deal primarily with three separate conditions, although I have also embodied a general clause. The first one governs the rule under which these regulations are formed and presented. I sent this resolution in to the Clerk early in October, and yet it 'bears the number 22. I have another one that I sent in in December, and possibly it may never be reached. I quite understand that the Clerk must maintain some order of precedence, and he takes the notices of motion in the order in which he receives them. I do not quarrel with that either; there must be some way of establishing precedence in placing the notices of motion on the order paper. But what I sought to change was the method by which past governments, or the government of the day, arbitrarily say in the House "There will be no more private members' days", which kills all the resolutions then on the order paper. I do not think that is a fair or desirable position. What I suggest as a substitute is of a two-fold character. We know that many of these resolutions are put on the order paper more or less as an expression of opinion, and really are not intended to be 27|
taken up. We can easily conceive of a case in which the government itself might have a notice of motion put on the order paper dealing with a matter which they did not want discussed and by the compliance of the member in whose name notice was given it would be passed on every occasion when it was called. In this way it would be possible to prevent that subject being discussed in the House. There is something wrong with rules which make that possible. I do not say this is being invoked to-day by the present government, but it is possible to do it. Now, my suggestion is that the resolutions should be-placed on the order paper as they are at present, but that when a motion is called and the member in whose name it stands is not prepared to go on with them, the motion should be dropped from the order paper. That does no injustice to the member concerned; he can give two days' notice and the resolution is restored to the order paper again but at the foot of the list. But it does ensure that a member who puts a resolution on the order paper in a bona fide manner and with the desire to go on with it will have some chance to proceed. Last year I had a resolution on the order paper but it was never reached because batches of these resolutions were called again and again, in some cases as many as six times, and the hon. members in charge of them did not take them up. Then, along about the time when he saw his opportunity was lapsing a member would get up and speak. My suggestion would be that if a member was not prepared to go on with a motion he has given notice of from two to three months, and even as long as four and five months beforehand, he cannot very well complain if his motion is dropped and he has to begin all over again. That would ensure whatever member was ready at least a decent chance to present his resolution. The suggestion I was going to make in that regard is this:	Instead of saying that on a
certain date all members' days would be cut off I would have it provided that, one month, if you like, or two months, after the opening of the session, no more notices of motion should be accepted. We should then know what to expect; but the motions that were then on the order paper would be afforded one opportunity at least of being dealt with. That, would ensure that every motion could be-heard; and yet it would not prolong to. an extreme degree the period within which those motions could be discussed. I merely-throw this out as a suggestion to be discussed by the committee.
Rules oj the House

I wanted to call attention to the necessity for the other change which is set out in my resolution:
2. Consider the advisability of changing the rules of the House to permit of debate on a motion to accept or reject an amendment made by the Senate to a Bill passed by the House.
I am aware-at least I am informed-that debate is allowed on a question of that kind provided it is what is called an order of the day; that is to say, if a day has elapsed between the time the message has been received from the Senate and the time when it is discussed in this House, then it becomes an order of the day and can be debated by any hon. member. But we well know that the most of these amendments made or rejected by the Senate come into this House in the very closing days of the session, when all rules are practically suspended, and nine times out of ten they never become an order of the day. I have a distinct recollection of a case a couple of years ago when a most important bill dealt with by the House and of great interest to many hon. members was rejected either in whole or in part by the Senate, and it was brought down not as an order of the day but simply as a message, and the minister in charge had the alternative of moving the acceptance or rejection of the amendment, and his speech was the only one allowed; the matter was not open to debate. I think that practice should be changed.
Those are practically all the precise amendments I propose, but I have a clause in my motion which would allow any question in connection with these subjects to be considered. If the government would allow the amalgamation of the resolution of the hon. member for Bast Calgary (Mr. Irvine) with my motion it might be a settlement of the whole question. Perhaps the hon. member for East Calgary would agree to the matter being referred to the select committee on Standing Orders instead of a special committee.

Possibly the views of all hon. members would be satisfactorily met if the government were agreeable to the appointment of a special committee, associating with the work of that committee his Honour the Speaker of the House. That the said resolution be amended by striking out the words "a revision of the rules is desirable, and that for this purpose", in line two, and substituting for the words "and report upon such revision at this session" in lines three and four, the words "jointly with Mr. Speaker the desirability of revising the rules of this House and to report to this House this session".
Then the motion would read:
That in the opinion of this House a special committee should be appointed to consider jointly with Mr. Speaker the desirability of revising the rules of this House and to report to this House this session.
It would seem to be appropriate that Mr. Speaker should be a member of any committee that is called upon to consider a revision of the rules.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
It seems rather anomalous that a motion to amend the rules should be moved by an hon. member who in moving it is out of order in violating the rules as they exist. I may take occasion to offer a few remarks on the rules as they are, and on some of the observations that the mover of the main resolution has made, as well as on some observations made by other hon. members.
The last revision of the rules of parliament took place in 1910. I believe that revision was made by a. special committee acting with the Speaker of the House of that time. There was a subsequent change of the rules in 1913, but that change was specific and did not involve any general revision. The rules therefore as they stand in substance are of fifteen years' duration, and it would be indeed surprising if in that period of time there were no way in which they could be improved. I am not one of those who feel that our rules are fundamentally wrong or that there is any grave injustice liable to be done to any section of this House on account of any of the main rules, or indeed minor ones, as they exist today. The mover of the motion bases his attack upon the existing state of affairs upon the inability of the third or fourth party in this House to move a sub-amendment in the budget debate; that is, to the motion tlo go into Ways and Means for the purpose of discussing the budget. This has already received some attention at the hands of parliament. Perhaps I cannot add to what I said at the time it was under discussion before, but I must say, as representing one of the three major parties here, that I have never felt in any discussion disability because of the rule as it exists, and I would deprecate a change in this respect; because a change allowing a second motion on an amendment to Supply, or Ways and Means, will undoubtedly lengthen the session of parliament and cause a loss of time. I do not know really what is going to be gained. It is true that in that special debate the exact position of each of three or four parties cannot be stated in the form of an amendment, only the position of two, the mover of the motion -that is the Finance minister-and whichever party chooses or has the opportunity to ad-

Rules oj the House
vance its amendment. I presume it would probably be the decision of Mr. Speaker that if the official opposition choose to avail itself of the occasion, it alone should have that privilege. I think only on one occasion in the three years that now have elapsed since this government came into power has the official opposition chosen to avail itself of the occasion. This has meant that other parties have exercised the right. Now last year, when the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) chose to move an amendment, I was favoured with a great deal of sympathy from the press of the country in having been out-manoeuvred by one of the newer members of the House. But I must frankly say that I felt myself wholly unworthy of that sympathy, and that it was unnecessary. There are numerous appropriate occasions when the position of any party in this House on the budget or on any other subject can be stated in the form of a resolution or amendment. The House goes into committee of Supply scores of times each session and on each motion for Supply it is open to any member representing a party, or any member representing only himself, to move such an amendment as he may choose; consequently there is really no disability. There is nothing gained by having them all on the one motion; they can come again. But the opportunities for delay are multiplied if amendments, sub-amendments, substitutional motions, and so forth, are allowed u,pon a motion for Supply. May I add, that I do not want to take any step-I hope I will be considered as sincere, especially as I am in opposition- I do not want to take any step which gives encouragement to multiplication of groups in this House of Commons. That may be an unpopular assertion, and I will give my special reasons for saying so. I do not think the group system is consonant with the British system of parliamentary government. I know I am powerless to prevent it; I do not pretend to stand at the shore and with a wave of my hand drive back the billows; but I think my influence and that of those who have regard for our institutions should be exerted to the utmost of our power toward this end. I do not think the multiplication of groups is consonant with the British system in any country; I do not believe it has worked successfully at all in France where the British system has been copied; but of all countries in the civilized world where there is embodied in it real peril to the state, none is so conspicuous an example as this Dominion. The group system in this Dominion is almost inevitably certain to become a system of sectional representation. I do not think the liability to sectional representation runs nearly as dangerously in the direction of occupational division as in the direction of geographical division. Speaking at this time I put myself in the judgment of hon. members when I say that after the next general election, this House of Commons, in so far as it is a collection of groups, will, in the main, represent geographical divisions. Here we have a country whose portions are widely separated, consequently, the points of view of whose peoples are widely different. We have a country further separated in its sections than any other country in the world to-day, and I do not exaggerate when I say that group representation on geographical division in this House spells more than difficulty, it spells very grave danger to this Dominion. Consequently, merely to accommodate the situation and to encourage representation by groups is no argument to my mind for amending the rules in this respect.
The hon. member further urges that there should be more latitude in the way of permission to private members to move for the expenditure of money. To this I am wholly and decisively opposed. Were I in the government I certainly would have offered much stronger objection than I have so far heard from any member of this government. I do not believe the confidence of the solid people in the country can be preserved if the right of private members of committees is to be countenanced to come into parliament and put parliament in the position of voting against appropriations here and there when they know that the vote itself does not mean commitment of the government, does not mean commitment of the treasury. It is inherent in our present system o.f government, if it is to be a success at all, if there is to be anybody at the helm steering the ship of state, that the government and the government alone should initiate expenditure. When I say "initiate expenditure", I mean to take such a step as commits the honour of parliament to that expenditure. You cannot beat the devil around the bush by having a committee come in and declare the moral liability of the nation, to be followed by a hasty motion to accept, with the government thereby finding that parliament has given it a mandate. This simply means the undermining of governmental responsibility. If we are to amend the rules further than we have done, I am certain this is going to result in an impairment of confidence in parliament, and, indeed, in the management of our country generally. I go further. I think the rule as it exists has been interpreted too generous-
Rules of the House

iy. In fact, I feel that the interpretation already given goes far to impair the efficacy of the rule, and that accounts for much of the difficulty into which we have been plunging; accounts, indeed, for the general losing of control of the financial policy of this House.
Another argument urged by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) is this, that there should be, on the part of the House, power to move amendments, especially in the estimates, without involving the fate of the government itself. That power exists. I do not think I differ at all from the viewpoint of the Prime Minister, if I understood correctly his utterance of some months ago, [DOT]when I say that an adverse vote in committee of this House on any estimate does not involve the fate of the government. Now I come to the suggestion by the hon. member for East Calgary that the rules should be amended so as to provide that the government should not have a majority on all committees of this House. If I were a member of the government I would feel bound to oppose the suggestion, and consequently I could not consistently support it now. I do not want ever to be a -party to the withdrawal from any administration of the measure of responsibility that an administration only can carry, and when I do not want to be a party to that, I must be a party to giving the government such rights as will enable it properly to carry that responsibility. Consequently it seems to me right and proper that any administration should have a majority on the committees of this House. What I complain of under present conditions, and I am not sure that it can be remedied, is this. Under the group system as we have it to-day the opposition not only is in a minority but it is almost extinguished in all committees of the House. There is only one opposition; hon. members to my left stand in holy horror at the mere intimation that they are an opposition of the government. So that so far from having nine-twentieths of the membership of a committee we are reduced to three-twentieths, and the government virtually has the other seventeen.

Always to oppose mis-government, yes; and that is all we do. Hon. members to my left had ah opportunity to become the official opposition and to choose when they would oppose, but memories of the days of old and of gallant battles together prevented -their assuming any position of the kind. But what I refer to is a disability which I do not know that it is in the power of the government to cure consistently with that measure of control which appertains to and should be enjoyed by all administrations.
The hon. member for Comox-AIbemi (Mr. Neil) takes a -much more moderate stand, and in the main I agree with what he says. I do not contend that the rules are perfect in every respect, but it seems to me that there might be an amendment to ensure better expedition at -times. The feature of the rules to which the hon. member refers as admitting of judicious amendment is one that might well be considered: that is to say, the presence of a motion standing in the name of a private member precludes the debate of another motion covering the same ground, and consequently it may foe used, as I myself am suspicious it has been used, as a means not of ensuring but of preventing debate on that very subject. I hasten, however, to assure hon. members to my left that in respect of my resolution now on the order paper the government has not asked that it be put on to ensure that at shall not be discussed-. The hon. member for Co-mox-Albemi suggests this remedy: First of all, he would prevent a private member's resolution being retained after, I think he said, two -months; and secondly, he would have a resolution automatically dropped after it had 'been twice passed without being debated. I am not sure that either method would appeal to me as the best. The refusal of a private member to take up a resolution on the order paper' d-oes not seem to me to be necessary at any stage of the session; I think he -should have the right to go ou, and if he fails to do so it is his own fault and he should take the consequences of any criticism -that might ensue. And) ithe compelling of a resolution to be dropped after being called twice without response would only put the -member in this position, that after -two days' notice he could put the resolution on the order paper again and then assert all the autocratic power which he exercised before.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
Anyone who
takes even a casual look at the architectural structure of this chamber must conclude at once that it was dedicated -to the medieval superstition of a two-party government. It is a two-party chamber, and the conception underlying its arrangement arises out of that idea, an idea that dates back to the time when the two parties composing parliament were so destructive to each other's policies and so bitterly opposed that they actually had to have a club lying on the table to keep anything like peace between them. And not only the architecture of the chamber, but the arrangement of its furniture as well, points to the same fact. I think it is a mistake that the arrangements of this House should con-
Rules of the House

demn the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition to the uncongenial task of looking each other in the face all the time. It seems to me that for the expeditious passage of business through the House it would be more reasonable for the Prime Minister and his colleagues to be further down the chamber. And when we come to the rules and practices, and the traditions of the House, some improvement might also be effected. But the really serious thing about parliamentary practices such as those with which we are encumbered is that they defeat the very purpose of parliament, namely, the transaction of public business in the interests of the people. We are the representatives of the people here and our business is to transact the public business in the interests of those people, and it would seem to me that the rules of the House are not conceived at all with that end in view. In fact, if I rightly judge the procedure of the House, the rules are meant to foster a procedure which in its working out obstructs public business instead of advancing it. In the passing of the estimates so far this session we have had examples of that. No impartial observer could honestly say that the passing of supply so far has redounded to the credit of the rules and practices of this House. There has been a lot of time wasted already by frivolous questions put to the minister, not with the object of eliciting information regarding his department, but obviously in an attempt to hamper him. The passing of Supply is one of the principal reasons for our being here-to superintend <he expenditure of the people's money; and any change in the rules that will make our superintendence more thorough is, I think, greatly to be desired, therefore to my mind the resolution of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) is a timely one.
It seems to me that the objections raised against it are all based upon the assumption that we are destined for all time to be pinned down to a two-party system. Even the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) appears to d'esire-almost unbecomingly as an independent-to bolster up that system. I do not propose to pay unreasoning deference to the two-party system, notwithstanding the view of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). He reminds me somewhat of a certain lady with a broom, when he says that he is going to stand against the emergence of the group system. I think that is a rash challenge. After all, what does the group system signify? It signifies the futility of the system that preceded it. It means that the system which has obtained' hitherto has 
been ineffectual in giving expression to the will of the people. Apparently there are a good many hon. members who do not realize that the government of this or any other country is an exceedingly more complex thing than it was when the old-party system was first started, that immensely complex character of our civilization to-day necessitates a variety of economic and political expression, and that it is certain, especially in a country like this, that we shall have in the future groups in this House. As to the prediction that the group system will lead to sectionalism, I would say that sectionalism as it obtains in Canada to-day is the fruit of the system that is being superseded. The group system has not yet been given a trial in this country. There are three groups in this House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: There are five.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
Well, there are numerous nascent groups as well as the actual. That is significant too, for a lot of those little buds and sprouts may eventually reach full development. But it is futile for the leader of the opposition to blame on us what is evidently the outgrowth of the effete two-party system which has been trying to run this country. He says that it is contrary to the British system. Well, so much the worse for the British system. But what is the British system? It is a conception that exists in the right hon. gentleman's mind as regards the best kind of parliamentary government which will further the peculiar political ideas for which he stand's. His so-called British system has no other existence. It is purely a figment of his imagination, something that in all its traditions and rules and practices is the best fitted to bolster privilege in this country. The greatest political genius could not evolve a party system better designed to uphold special privilege in this country. I repeat, if the coming group system is contrary to the British system, then so much the worse for the British system. But it is not contrary to the true British system, because that system is born of a spirit which always proves itself capable of the fullest adaptation to the changing conditions of the people; anything that shuts its eyes to developing conditions is antiquated and is contrary to the British system. And the aspersion cast upon the group in this corner of the House that we are always kowtowing to the party opposite ranks with the assertion that the group system is contrary to the British system. Our purpose in being here is to prove that the differences and distinctions that are supposed to exist between the parties under the old system are purely make-believe, and

Rules oj the House
I think the interruption of the hon. gentleman was a timely one. You have to get back into our committee rooms to find out just where the kowtowing is done. After all, the people are not interested in knowing just how many times we vote with the party opposite or with the party on our right; but they are interested! in the fidelity with which we try to carry out their will, and no matter whether in the banking or any other committee where we have been face to face with the machinations of special privilege this group has never been found wanting yet. The distinctive thing about this group is that it has stood four square many a time against special privilege in opposition to the solid support given to special privilege by the old two-party system.
Therefore I think the resolution is a timely one. The present development of our parliamentary system has been through the gradual accretion of rules and practices that had been adopted for some particular reason or another, but it is only rational to suppose that periodically this growing tree should need a certain amount of pruning in order to serve its purpose-that of facilitating the business of the people.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, the rules of this House have been founded not on imagination but on practice, and have come down to us in the main from the Mother of Parliaments. It will be found that every rule, though it may not be perfect, is based on experience, and nearly every session we discover additional reasons for certain rules that we had either lost sight of or were not aware of before. So they cannot be altered lightly, and I do not think this House has any idea of altering them lightly.
My hon. friend (Mr. Bird) who has just sat down spoke of group government, in reply to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen); but I suppose the people will say whether we are to have group government or not. Personally I am in favour of the two old parties, or of two parties at all events, not the "old" ones because I think they are as young as those that are called younger; but I am in favour of two parties as the best system of government. But that is for the people to say, not for me.

speechtext:
The suggestion has been
made that the Progressive party has favoured this government. Well really I do not see how they could help it, and I am in earnest in that. The progressive measures of this government, though called Liberal, are still Progressive, a great many of them, and although on occasions the Liberal government and its supporters could not see their way to go all the distance with the Progressives, sometimes perhaps only a short distance, at all events the government went further than hon. gentlemen opposite, and consequently if the Progressives voted at all they would have to support those who came nearer to their ideals. I do not see how a Progressive could go home and ask Progressive electors for their support if he had done anything else.
I just want to mention one or two other matters, and first as to sectional discussions. I agree with the leader of the opposition to a large extent that all over Canada, even among members of the two former parties there is a disposition to form ourselves into geographical units. Deputations come to the government every day from different parts of Canada, with sectional views; I am not using the word in any derogatory sense, but we seem to have got away from the idea of the old Fathers of Confederation that we are to make a great Canada of this country by, if you will, a policy of compromises, so far as that is necessary, between the different parts of this country. I think we are making a mistake; I do not say it is the Progressive party that is doing it, but day -by day ministers of the crown are approached from the angle of only one part of Canada. This is right in a sense, because each part of Canada has its own difficulties and peculiar problems, but after all, the government and parliament ought to do the same thing, and that is to take into consideration all these sectional viewpoints, and then arrive as closely as possible at a common working basis for every province in the Dominion of Canada. That is the only way we can manage to make Canada great and bring prosperity again to this country, and *when there is prosperity in a country, contentment follows. I do not want to- go any further along that line except to relate a little incident that occurred eight
jRules of the House

or ten or eleven years ago. Three gentlemen -I think I have repeated this in the House before-were sitting in a car, one of them the late Sir Wilfrid, and each was asked to suggest what might be a difficulty in the future in Canada. Sir Wilfrid thought that the great desire of Canadians, and 5 p.m. it was a question they would be called upon to deal with practically, ought to be to get a united people, free from prejudice one against the other, throughout the Dominion of Canada. Another suggested that our problem of the future would be our Imperial relations. I had the honour to suggest, that I thought perhaps one of the things we would be called upon to discuss in a few years in a practicable way would be the differences that might arise in this Dominion between the east and the west. These are all practical questions, and we cannot approach any of them from an absolutely sectional viewpoint. If we do we are doomed for failure. I would like in the years that I have to be in public life, and they may be a great many-

We are trying to look

Perhaps everybody is to blame by having a slightly sectional view, and if you will allow me to say it, I think perhaps we have been doing it in the last year or two more than ever before, that is, getting up and defending not Canada with all her works but that little part of Canada in which we live. While that is necessary, the vision will have to broaden out if we are to have a greater Canada.
Perhaps I am getting away from the rules a little. As to the responsibility of the government, I have always taken strong ground. I do not know whether I am an old Tory in doing so or not, but I have always taken

strong ground on the responsibility of government, to a large extent, for what emerges from parliament. True, I would not interfere with the right of parliament to be supreme, even though a government can be put out by parliament under our constitution, which cannot be done in the United States.
The leader of the opposition has referred to committees bringing in reports. I am free to admit that we ought to be more careful with those reports.

speechtext:
We get a number of men
on a committee, and I put myself in with the rest, and they work on a certain question day after day and become absolutely enthusiastic over it, perhaps to the neglect of other questions, and then bring in a report which will meet the views of the men who have been pursuing this one question in which they have become enthusiastically interested. Now this House should not approve of that report without the closest scrutiny, because it might involve something that would be of detriment to the entire Dominion of Canada.
As to referring the estimates to a committee, that is a question that is debatable. You will say:	You have done it yourself. Yes,
we are trying an experiment, but, remember, that experiment is not with the general affairs of Canada, but concerns only two institutions, mercantile enterprises upon which Canada has entered. They are not quite in the same class with the ordinary expenditure, of a government. The government has to take a stand in the House as to what wiii be considered a want of confidence motion. I do not say that defeat in Supply, unless it might be on a vote involved by some large question of policy on the part of the government, ought to be taken as a want of confidence vote; but if it involves defeat on a large question of policy for the government, for which we are asking money, I would say it ought to be taken as a want of confidence motion. There is this point to consider. Put a government in a position such as I have indicated, and if you were to take the view that no vote in committee or even in the House should be taken as a vote of want of confidence, unless the mover should so declare, it would be impossible for any government to carry on its business. The position of that government before the country would be so humiliating that they would have to resign. And the mere fact that a member says "I am going to move this resolution; I am sorry to put you in a predicament and humiliate you before the country but I do

Rules oj the House
not mean it as a vote of want of confidence'' does not relieve the situation. In the great majority of instances my own view, as the result of years of experience, is that we cannot help but regard the vote as one of want of confidence.
Now. I would suggest that one or two amendments might be made, not to the rules but to the standing orders. The hon. member for Nelson (l\lr. Bird) suggested the point that in committee of Supply there should be nothing placed in the way of hon. members getting all the information that is necessary. But perhaps we all overstep the mark sometimes by prolonging discussion without getting any information. I am not sure that there might be two ways of curtailing that practice. One would be to not have any Hansard at all in committee.

speechtext:
I am coming to that. There is no special rule for the minister. I am the greatest sinner in the House in regard to lengthy speaking. I have made the longest speech that was ever delivered in the House of Commons, so I can talk freely of myself. I am not sure that the work of parliament would not be expedited if the length of our speeches even with the Speaker in the chair were limited. There is no question to my mind that if parliament were deeply interested in any question it would admit of exceptions being made to this rule unanimously. If there was some subject demanding a longer period than that named in the rules parliament is not critical to that extent, but by unanimous consent either the leader of the opposition, or the Prime Minister, or any member who had some topic that required quite a length of time to develop would get permission from parliament to speak at greater length. But this
change would curtail the amount of time we use in discussing some of the minor questions at least.
I want to conclude with this other reference:
I am a kind of ritualist, I would not want to get away from any of our rules lightly because there is reason for them all; and unless some good reason could be given for any deviation I believe that making as little change as possible in the general rules will conduce to our conducting business with decorum. It is true we cannot get away from the fact that conditions have changed. The rules were largely made,-some of the sections at any rate-with the idea of there being only two parties in the House. There may be some reason for having a number of minor changes because nothing develops the need for changes like experience, and experience may have shown that we ought to have some changes. I am quite willing for a special committee to look into the rules of the House and advise with Mr. Speaker to see if there be a necessity of revising the rules in some respects; but I would suggest to the committee that they do not enter upon the work of revision with any idea that they are going to tear the rules of the House all to pieces and substitute new rules, because the old1 ones have done splendid service. With the exception perhaps of needing some slight revision I would not like to see the principle of those rules altered very much.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
I do not intend to delay the House more than a few minutes in replying. I think the discussion has perhaps taken a course that would have been more appropriate in a committee that had met to consider the revision of the rules but that was doubtless due to the method of presentation which I adopted. It was necessary for me to give some indication of what I understood to be the possibility of revising a rule of the House with some definiteness. I therefore presented my own ideas on those matters, but not with any hope that hon. members would agree with my particular suggestions. I only used those in the way of illustration in trying to establish the need for a special committee. Some hon. members, however, appear to have concluded that the debate is on the nature of the amendments that may be made, rather than being as it is a debate on the advisability of appointing a committee. My object in using those illustrations was merely to set forth the need for the committee.
I do not intend to enter into the arguments that have been advanced, further than to make a comment on the observations which have been offered in regard to the group system. I
Rules of the House

had no intention of course of introducing that idea in proposing the argument, 'but I can see how it is certainly relevant to the discussion. The right hon. leader of the opposition does not believe that the group system is going to have any future, and he does not think that it ought to. I do not know, of course, that it is going to have any future or not, I hope that it will. But there is one way of getting rid of some of the groups in this House, and that is for the Conservative party to join .-.he Labour party, or for the Liberal party to join the Progressive party.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
I do not hear the Conservative party very loud in their expression of willingness to come over here and join the Labour party. They cannot expect that we will go over there and join the Conservative party or cross the floor and join the Liberal party, because whether we have an idea or not we think we have and that is the same thing, so far as the reason for the existence of a group is concerned. As to the sectional idea and the geographical ideas, which have been mentioned, these exist whether you have one party, two parties or one hundred parties; and I venture to say that one of the problems which the government party have to deal with at the present time, is that very sectional problem. That would be no more difficult to deal with under fifty groups than under one group. We do not create any sectionalism by merely representing it. If it were not there it could not be represented. To try and hush those things up by maintaining, through artificial means, the two-party system is not, in my opinion, the way to meet the situation.
I want to make one remark in reference to what was said by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He very properly pointed out that there was a reason for every one of the rules of this House. I am sure I never doubted that, but it is just possible that some of the reasons which once existed for those rules are not very relevant now, and it is also just possible, as was pointed out I think by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), that some of the reasons for these rules might be very much opposed to the best interests of the people to-day. But it certainly was not my intention to give the impression that I looked' upon those rules lightly, or thait I had sought to slight them in any way whatsoever, nor do I look forward to any tearing up of these rules on the part of the committee which I hope will be appointed. I certainly doubt whether any committee would be prepared to go very far beyond what was

suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighem) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I agree with the proposals that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni made. I would be willing to go much further myself, but I do not expect the House will accept my leadership in such a matter. If it did, it would certainly go much beyond the stage marked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I have been very much pleased with the discussion as far as it has gone. I certainly am prepared to withdraw my motion in preference to the amendment which was movedl by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I think his amendment covers thoroughly rvhat I was seeking to establish. Therefore, in favour of the amendment of the hon. Prime Minister, I ask leave to withdraw my motion.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. IRVINE FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
I desire to make a few remarks from the point of view of a young member coming into the supposedly complicated maze of parliamentary procedure, coming here as a freshman in knowledge of the procedure and in knowledge of the parliamentary difficulties which I suppose we will be confronted with. From my personal experience

and I have taken some part in the activities of parliament -I have not found that the rules fetter one's activity. I have not found that there has not been almost every opportunity offered for any proposal or any idea which I had wanted to place before parliament, or that I was confronted) with any serious obstacle. I believe, however, that a committee such as outlined by the Prime Minister to look into this question and to inquire into the problems and matters which the various speakers have referred to would be advantageous to the members of the House and to the procedure in the future. But if this committee approaches its task with the idea of enabling the government- and the Progressive party to carry on before the country the appearance of -being opposed to each other, while at the same time they are conducting the business in the House, in the corridors of the buildings and in the policies of the government in a way which finds agreement, but which, in the idea of the party in this part of the chamber, is opposed to the proper procedure of parliament, then I would not be in favour of very serious activities on the part of the committee. In other words, it would appear from the remarks of members of the government and some of our friends to the left that the real intent behind this resolution is to enable these parties to join more closely in that

Mountain Freight Scale
matrimonial relationship which does not seem to have a legal status. When it comes to the encouragement of sectional or group representation in parliament, I would be opposed to it. I do not think that my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) can claim to be entirely a representative of labour. Over one-half of my constituency is largely labour, and I believe I have the honour of representing labour in the House of Commons and of speaking in their best interests. This idea of representing a class group in my judgment is a mistaken one. A member entering parliament has the obligational responsibility of representing all classes in his constituency, and the truth of the matter is that the two old parties are non-class, and they attempt to, and in fact do, represent their constituents as a whole, and are open in mind and conviction to the interests of all the sections of the constituency, with the idea of harmonizing these interests and expressing the will of the majority of the people in their ridings. But if this committee carry on their work in such a way as to make more easy the co-operation between the government and my friends to the left, or if they carry on their work with an idea of developing group government or sectional interests, then I say that history has proven that the policies and practices of the old party system really are the best for the advancement of our democratic institutions. There is no doubt about that. Some constitutions are made specially for group governments. Take France or the United States for example; there the constitution is framed in such a manner that members stay there for a certain length of time, and no matter how a vote goes in congress in the United States, or in the Chamber of Deputies in France, no matter whether adverse or favourable, the government continues and remains in power, subject to certain methods by which governments are changed; but they are not the same principles as we have here. In fact, in my judgment we have the most democratic method, the most efficient method of enabling the will of the majority of the people to be made effective immediately in policy and in legislation; and so I repeat, in carrying on the work of this committe so far as the rules of the House are concerned, I hope that the committee will have regard for experiences of the past, and that they will be imbued with a solemn and strong conviction to maintain the principles, the rules which we already have, and that they will not take any action which will tend to develop a group system of government.
Amendment (Mr. Mackenzie King) agreed to.
Motion as amended, agreed to.
