speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. KENNEDY (West Edmonton) moved:
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the mountain freight scale should be abolished in so far as it is reflected in standard mileage rates, class rates and commodity rates.
He said: We have in Canada five rate territories. For the purpose of our discussion this afternoon three of them are important: that is the Atlantic territory, which includes territory from the Atlantic to as far west as Sudbury; the prairie territory which begins at and includes Port Arthur and reaches west to points just east of the Rocky mountains and the Pacific or mountain territory which commences at the western boundary of the prairie territory. The other two territories are the Superior territory and the British Columbia lakes, but these two latter are not so important for the purpose of our present discussion. All articles of freight in Canada fall into the general Canadian classification of ten classes. There are six additional classes, running from one and one-half times the first class up to four and one-half times first class, and all articles of freight in Canada come under those sixteen classes. Of course, as there are different rate territories with rates varying in one territory as compared with another, it will be seen that even with a uniform classification freight rates in one portion of Canada are higher or lower, as the case may be, than in another. Generally speaking, freight rates in the Atlantic territory are lower than freight rates in the prairie territory, and freight rates in general in the mountain territory are higher than in the prairie territory.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
estimate that per mile, or how?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
During the
discussion I want to give to the minister and the House my reason for thinking that there is that difference. I am not going to rely upon mileage comparisons of rates because mileage comparisons are somewhat tricky, but I will take the declared opinion of the Board of Railway Commissioners over the last twenty years. I also intend, in the course of my argument, to develop reasons why the Board of Railway Commisisoners cannot deal with this question satisfactorily and really give us the equalization that we ought to have in Canada.
Mountain Freight Scale

Various protests have been made from time to time with regard to this discrimination between the different territories, but the discrimination has been allowed to continue. The Board of Railway Commissioners has dealt with the question time and again, and in connection with various rate cases it has declared that unquestionably in its opinion, there was discrimination, but it was not unjust nor unfair. The Railway Act, of course, states that there shall be no unjust nor undue discrimination, and the board in its investigations and findings has found that although there is a lower rate in eastern Canada tnan in the west and a lower rate on the prairies than in the mountains, the discrimination was not unjust nor undue because of conditions obtaining in those various territories. The mountain scale, until recently, has been looked upon as distinctly a British Columbia handicap or problem, and it may be that prior to a few years ago, before the Panama canal was opened and elevators were constructed at Vancouver and before the trade on the prairies began to move more directly through British Columbia, out on to the Pacific, to the Old Land and to the Orient, it was not such an important question for the prairies. The prairies right through to the Peace river country had been looked upon largely as tributary to Fort William, Port Arthur, Montreal and eastern Canada generally. But the development during the last years, the opening of the Panama canal, the jelevator construction at Vancouver and making possible thereby the shipping of grain by that route, has made this question one of vast importance for the prairie provinces as well as for British Columbia. So within the last two years, we find Alberta associating herself with British Columbia in a protest against some at least of those mountain rates. The western rates case began in 1911 and judgment was delivered on April 6, 1914. The complaint was:
1.	That the tolls charged in the provinces of western Canada, (Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta) are higher than those charged in eastern Canada, (Ontario and Quebec), and
2.	Of unjust discrimination by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in tolls from Vancouver, British Columbia, to interior points in the western provinces as compared with the tolls charged to the same points in eastern Canada.
The Board of Railway Commissioners de-Lvered its judgment, and on page 156 of Canadian Railway Cases, volume 17, we find this:
On the issue of discrimination there is no doubt whatever that disparity of rates exists. While the railway companies plead a greater diversity of traffic, better traffic conditions and return loads, and a lower wage

schedule in the east than in the west, there is to my mind no question but that those different factors and their effects are of necessity mirrored in the companies' returns, and are more than compensated for by the long average haul and lower terminal expenses that obtain in the west.
Practically the same thing was said afterwards in the judgment delivered by the board in eastern rates case on June 6, 1916. The reference is to Canadian Railway Cases, volume 22, page 41. The judgment states:
While, as has been set out at greater length in the western rates case, differences of conditions do exist between eastern and western Canada, and while western freight rates have already materially been reduced, the general schedule there obtaining is still higher, notwithstanding the fact that certain western rates that may be instanced are lower. There is no doubt but what the act requires and the general public interest of the country as a whole demands, that, if practicable, eastern rates should be advanced so that the different schedules may more nearly approach a parity.
I am aware that an absolute parity is impracticable, but, as conditions become similar, a reasonable parity ought to be obtained.
The next case to which I refer is the 40 per cent increase case. During 1922, before the committee on railway transportation costs, it seems to me that the railway representatives made a strenuous effort to convince the committee that rates after all were very nearly equal as between eastern Canada and the prairies prior to the 40 per cent increase. In the 40 per cent increase caise, the judgment, which was delivered in December, 1920, has this to say:
Allowing for the undoubted fact that a very large proportion of the traffic both east and west is on the commodity basis, I am still forced to the conclusion that the rates in western Canada average considerably greater than in the east, possibly around 15 or 18 per cent.
In coming to this conclusion I am stating nothing new, as this fact has always been recognized and particularly by Sir Henry Drayton, the then chief commissioner, in the Eastern Rates case, so called In re Eastern Tolls. 22 Can. Ry. Cases, at page 41, where the following statement appears:-
"While, as has been set out at greater length in the Western Rates case, differences of condition do exist between eastern and western Canada, and while western freight rates have already materially been reduced, the general schedule there obtaining is still higher, notwithstanding the fact that certain western rates that may be instanced are lower. There is no doubt but what the act requires and the general public interest of the country, as a whole, demands, that, if practicable, eastern rates should be advanced so that the different schedules may mare nearly approach a parity".
As a 40 per cent increase was given in eastern Canada and a 35 per cent in western Canada, that still left, in the opinion of the board, a considerable difference. Previous to this increase the difference in the two rate scales was approximately 15 or 18 per cent. Since that time there has been some reduction in rates both east and west. We had a.

Mountain Freight Scale
reduction in grain rates after the committee had reported to parliament in 1922, and then we had other reductions in the east which brought the rates down to within 17J per cent of what they had been previous to the 40 per cent increase, and in the west to 12i per cent above the rates in existence previous to September 1920.
The committee on railway transportation which considered the question whether or not it was advisable to reinstate the Crowsnest pass agreement had strong representations made to it in 1922, when it was pointed out that in the event of the rates being lowered on grain the Canadian Pacific Railway might be unable to pay its dividends. I submitted figures to the House last year to show that notwithstanding the reduction the Canadian Pacific Railway had better earnings in 1922 and 1923 from grain in western Canada than it had the previous year. This was no doubt due in part to the fact that we had splendid crops in western Canada during those two years. Figures were submitted, taken from the files of the Board of Railway Commissioners, relating to the net and gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the west. Going back to the years 1916 to 1922 we find that the operating revenues in the east amounted to $226,500,000 while in the west they amounted to $356,500,000, the west being 57^ per cent higher than the east. The operating ratio in the east was 73.3 and :n the west 57, while in the prairie west it was 54.5. The net earnings of the west were $92,500,000 greater than those of the east, or 154 per cent; that is to say, the net earnings in the east amounted to $60,000,000 and in the west to $152,500,000. From the years 1916 to 1920, before the period in which the increase ^ took place, the operating revenues were, in the east, $370,000,000 and in the west $442,000,000; so that the west was $72,000,000 more than the east, or 20 per cent. And this embraces the prosperous manufacturing war munition period an the east. I have not the division of operating revenues for the years 1922 and 1923; I have already stated that during the grain moving months there was a higher gross earning and a higher net profit than in the summer months for the year 1921.
I have here a statement for the year 1924 of the operating expenses and the net revenues of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I want to put this statement on record because some people seem to think that there was something unholy done to the rest of Canada in the reinstatement of the Crowsnest pass rates on grain and that it wiped out forever any discrimination between eastern and western rates. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in the various judgments handed down by the Board of Railway Commissioners we have the proof that the prairie west has been paying more than its share of profit to the railways. That the Canadian Pacific has a greater mileage in the three prairie provinces is not in itself an explanation of the fact that its net revenues are greater, because we know that the cost per mile of construction in eastern Canada is very much higher than that in the west. In the eastern rates case the railways applied for a general increase in rates, and the Board of Railway Commissioners decided they would have to take into consideration the position of the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk was an old-established railway, and the board decided, in a general way, that they would accept the valuation of the Grand Trunk as a basis on which to fix rates, and let the newer railways take their chance, as they would not have come into the territory unless they were

willing to compete with the railway already established there. It was admitted that a remunerative rate scale for the Grand Trunk would be all right for the Canadian Pacific, because the Canadian Pacific was in fact in a more prosperous condition at that time than the Grand Trunk. The claim was made that the capital charges of the Grand Trunk were no less than 8131,395 per mile of line. This value was not accepted by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and they made a comparison with various other lines to ascertain what might be a fair valuation. They found that the Glen Tay-Agincourt line of the Canadian Pacific cost altogether $13,144,685, or $71,547 per mile; the Intercolonial, according to the government statistics of 1915, cost $75,066 per mile, including equipment and terminals; the National Transcontinental cost $76,632 per mile; the Ontario Hydro-Electric line from Toronto to Guelph cost $100,000 per mile, including terminals. In its judgment, which will be found in volume 6 of the board's judgments, pages 153 and 146. appears the following:
If the cost of the National Transcontinental were applied to the Grand Trunk mileage, adding a conservative estimate of $10,000 a mile for equipment, a vaule of $86,632 per mile is arrived at.
When we compare that with the general cost of lines on the prairies, we find that the government guarantees ranged from $13,000 to $20,000 per mile. We know that was not the total cost, but we know also that when the government had something to do with building the mountain section they had to give a higher guarantee altogether. When the Grand Trunk Pacific bill was put through the guarantee for the prairie section, which was supposed to cover 75 per cent of the cost of the line, was $13,000 per mile, but in the mountains the guarantee was $30,000 per mile. I understand that this limitation regarding its mountain section, was afterwards wiped out. It is recognized that there is no comparison between the cost of building railways on the prairie territory and in the mountain territory, or the railways east and west of the prairies. So I submit that the tremendous earnings of the Canadian Pacific on the western prairie lines, is not explained by a greater mileage. This is offset by the fact that the cost of construction is much lower. This 'bears out the statement, which has been made time and again by the Board of Railway Commissioners, that in general the rates are higher in western than they are in eastern Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not arguing for the moment that there was anything unjust in this, but I do say that so far as that portion of the

prairies is concerned which is so situated geographically that it ought and does use the Pacific coast ports, if in the past it has been impossible to give that section rates based on the local cost of construction and of operation, it is absolutely unfair to continue charging us the mountain scale of rates-rates which are in excess of those on the prairie territory-where the grades are 'better and the cost of construction no higher than the maximum in eastern Canada. In 1907 when the British Columbia coast cities applied to the Board of Railway Commissioners to have the mountain scale wiped out, one of the arguments used in rebuttal was this: Vancouver and the Pacific coast cities have certain advantages due to water competition, they have low through rates westbound, and they should not complain if they have the disadvantages of their geographical position when they are shipping inland, over mountain, grades that cost more to construct. But so far as the province of Alberta and parts of western Saskatchewan are concerned, we are not allowed the advantage in our rates of the lower cost of construction and the lower cost of operation of the prairie lines, and we have heaped upon us the disadvantage of the mountain scale rates when we want to do business with that part of the country that our geographical position puts us in a position to do business with.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I had just finished giving some proof that the prairie provinces had been paying their share of railway profits, and possibly a little more, during the past twenty years or so. I should like to supplement that evidence by quoting an article from this morning's Ottawa Citizen:
New York, Feb. 22.-Over sixteen hundred members o,f the New York Traffic Club, and the largest gathering in the history of the organization, were present at the annual banquet in the Commodore hotel here last night, where E. W. Beatty, K.C., president and chairman of the Canadian Pacific Railway, was the chief speaker. The guests included the executives of many of the larger United States railroads. W. A. Schumacher, president of the club, was in the chair.
Mr. Beatty was accompanied by W. R. Mclnnes, of the C.P.R., Mr. Beatty largely devoted his remarks to a review of Canada's railway history, which was, he said, the story of great achievement, mistakes, failures and political and economic complications end-

ing with the most unique situation existing in the world to-day. He traced the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and said that the success of the company had provoked similar but over-ambitious enterprises. He referred to the Canadian Northern which, he said, while a great conception, carried to physical completion, had failed because it was built before its time and could not be operated successfully through the dislocation of war time.
"If," said the speaker, instead of turning its prairie lines into a portion of a transcontinental system, the owners had been content to make as their termini the mountains on the west, and the Great Lakes on the east, they would have been the wealthiest men in Canada, and Canada would not to-day be facing the railway burden it is compelled to bear."
The mountain scale, Mr. Speaker, is somewhat higher than the prairie scale. In 1907, by the judgment in connection with the British Columbia Pacific Coast Cities versus the Canadian Pacific Railway, the mountain scale on part of the mileage was reduced to within 100 per cent higher than the prairie scale and to about one and a half times the prairie scale on about 500 miles of the mountain mileage. At the time of the western rates case in 1916, the mountain scale was reduced to from one and a half to one as compared with the prairie scale on its full western mileage.	Since that time, in 1922, I
think it was, the mountain scale was reduced somewhat nearer to the prairie scale, but it still is somewhat higher than the prairie scale. As I have pointed out because of the development of trade routes via the Pacific coast and through the Panama canal, and the development of trade with the Orient, we are face to face with a problem where the prairies, being denied rates equal to those in the eastern part of Canada, where the cost of construction and operation is lower, have to pay higher charges when they want to ship over grades just as favourable as those in the east.
Of course, it is to Alberta's advantage to do business with British Columbia. The provinces of Alberta and British Columbia are largely complementary. We in Alberta grow wheat and produce cheese, butter and other commodities for export, and British Columbia requires a great many of these commodities. British Columbia manufacturers on the other hand, are able to cater to the market on the prairies, and if there is anything in the home market idea, and I think there is, it is to the mutual advantage of British Columbia and Alberta that they have favourable interprovincial rates, and thereby each helps in the development of the other. I think that the main hindrance to getting an equalization of rates has been the attitude taken by the Board of Railway Commissioners, that the railways must have their dividends. That principle broke down when they sought to apply it to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the 28
Canadian Northern. Though some compromise had been made in 1916 between the rates that were absolutely necessary on the Canadian Pacific and the rates necessary to keep the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern afloat, the railway commission were not able to save those railways from the financial difficulties into which they finally drifted.
Professor MacGibbon, of Edmonton, has written a book entitled Railway Rates and the Canadian Railway Commission, in which he says:
Xhe fundamental holding of the board is that there shall be a fair return on the funds actually invested in the enterprise. This position is emphatically taken in The Dawson Board of Trade vs The White Pass and Yukon Railway Company case.
The board had ordered certain reductions on the Yukon Railway, and the Yukon Railway appealed to the Privy Council. The Privy Council granted a rehearing. The company also applied to the board for the rescinding of its ord'er providing for a reduction in rates until such time as the rehearing was completed. The board in granting a stay until the rehearing said this:
The board never intended to deprive those carriers of the opportunity of earning, first, not only enough to pay the interest upon their bonds, but, secondly, to pay a fair return upon the actual capital that went into the road and that is now outstanding in the form of stock. No controlling commission has got, it seems to us, the right or the jurisdiction to make an order that would have the effect of destroying the earning power of the capital that honestly went into the facility-
And so on. A little further on in the judgment we find this:
Had the management been as economical then as now, with the large earnings in those days, no doubt substantial reductions could have been made without hardship upon the stockholders; but this matter can be dealt with only upon conditions as they exist today.
In connection with the same principle in the western rates case we find this:
The whole question is or should be what rates are fair? In considering this question of course surpluses earned by past operations may be evidence to the facts that the rates under which they were earned were exorbitant. Any industrial enterprise has the right to a reasonable surplus over and above its fixed charges and dividends. A railway is also entitled to a reasonable surplus. . . . To my mind it is quite impossible for the board to deal with rates in the west on the hypothesis that the Canadian Pacific is the only railway that should be taken into consideration.
Subsequent to that, however, in 1920 order No. 308 already referred to, was issued', in which the same position was taken that rates should be fixed and guaranteed that would enable the Canadian Pacific to pay 6 per cent, and then a surplus of 2 per cent to cover what might be called contingencies.

Now, I want to say this-it may be heresy to some but it seems to me to be common sense-I do not know that any railway corporation, or any other kind of corporation, should have its dividends guaranteed at the expense of the people of the country. I am willing to admit the importance of the Canadian Pacific, and the importance of the other railways of Canada; but when we find the president of the Canadian Pacific to-day contending for his dividends and his surplus I must say I cannot see that that concern is of any more importance to Canada than the industry of agriculture or the manufacturing industries of the Dominion. Such treatment might be justified under normal con-

ddtions, but during the last few years conditions have been abnormal; and if the Board of Railway Commissioners tries to fix rates on a basis that will guarantee its dividends and a surplus to the Canadian Pacific, it can only do so at the expense of the other industries of Canada. And what condition are these other industries in? I know that agriculture is not in a position to stand it; and I am told that in the case of a great many other industries not only are they earning no dividend's but that through the deflation of the last few years they have experienced a loss of from 50 to 75 per cent on their capital investment as well. Therefore, as far as I can see railway dividends should be no more sacred than dividends on capital invested in agriculture or in manufacturing concerns.
I have here a copy of the U.F.A. published in Calgary on February 2, 1925, on page 15 I find it stated:
Canada's railways must have a living profit.
Then it is stated in an advertisement:
No greater catastrophe could overtake Canada than the weakening of the present strong position of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
That seems to me an extraordinary statement. When you place dividends on one corporation representing an investment of less than a billion against those of all other industries representing almost twenty times that amount I say it is an utterly ridiculous statement. I believe we have to get away from the idea that the dividends or the interests of any corporation are to be held sacred. I am willing to give the Canadian Pacific-and any other corporation in Canada for that matter-all that we are entitled to as agriculturists and nothing more. I believe that we ought to have equality in so far as our treatment by the government of the country is concerned. I do not believe the Canadian parliament has any right to hand over authority to a commission of any kind, be it a railway commission or a tariff commission, to especially look after one industry when that can only be done at the expense of the rest of the people of the country.
There is another objection that I have to this mountain scale: It has overflown into the prairies. I suppose if we had never had the mountain scale through the Rocky mountains and out to the coast we should not likely have had it in the territory between Edmonton and the Peace river country. But we have a railway there built some years ago, and its grades are just as low as the grades of the Canadian National railway through the Yellowhead pass, 4/10 of one per cent grades, except crossing to the Smoky river and the

I would rather see the rates reduced and' then have the question dealt with after we saw the result, than to start in with an offer of a subsidy in order to get the rate reduction.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have said nearly enough on this question. KELLNER (East Edmonton): Mr. Speaker, I wish to endorse the sentiments of the member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Ladner) in support of this resolution, and I share his hope that we shall have an exhaustive discussion of the whole mountain rate structure. I too appreciate the futility of any such hope, when I look at the government benches and observe only three or four ministers present, two or three of whom I notice are watching the clock very closely and apparently intend to leave shortly. In my estimation parliament obtained the right at least to share in the fixing of rates away back in 1881 when certain subsidies were granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Since that time the country has entered into various undertakings with one railway company and another which I think beyond a shadow of a doubt consolidated our position, and it is *worth while for us to seriously consider why the government from time to time undertook to pay subsidies and to make land grants to various railway companies. It will not be seriously argued that there was any desire on the part of the country to make somebody a present by this means; undoubtedly a substantial consideration in return was involved. It was the opinion of the rank and file of the people that that assistance would eventually be a factor in reducing freight rates. I do not think there is any question that it was understood, if it was not expressed, that at a period of financial stringency, such as we are passing through at the moment, those money and land grants would be treated by the railway companies as being in lieu of dividends. But from the very start the policy seems to have been unsuccessful. Those who have studied the situation back in 1896 find that the western fanners at that time were actually hauling their grain much further than should have been necessary to reach the Northern Pacific in Manitoba, and there are numerous resolutions from boards of trade and other organizations and from private
Mountain Freight Scale

citizens protesting against the high freight rates and lack of transportation facilities that then prevailed. It was apparently the opinion of the country that the subsidy proposition had not been a success in bringing about low freight rates, and a new theory was advanced. It was suggested that the only way to control freight rates was by competition, and an agitation sprang up for the building of more railways, with the result that the country subsidized and bonused the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. But the coming of these railways did not bring about lower rates. I do not think there is any question that the cost of construction was deliberately made sufficiently high so that low freight rates would never be enjoyed in our day and generation.
Allow me to deviate for a moment to the election of 1911, which our friends to the right take a great deal of credit to themselves at having won against the other old party on what was to all intents and purposes a tariff question. But in western Canada I do not think the tariff entered into the election at all; the people there by their votes desired to protest against the method which had been used in financing the building of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. At any rate this was the case in my section of the country. When what are to-day our National lines were projected we were promised very much better grades across the mountains than the Canadian Pacific ever had, and were led to believe that that company's engineers had made a terrific blunder when they selected the southern route through the Kicking Horse pass; and as a corollary we were promised lower freight rates. We have got the easier grades, and on what used to be the Canadian Northern our National railways can draw as heavy loads east as they can west across the mountains, but we have never seen any reduction in our rates. I do not think that the railway commission or any other body that has ever investigated the situation has argued that the present mountain scale of rates is necessary so far as the Canadian National is concerned. In fact I think I am safe in saying that the president of our National system has admitted that the mountain scale of rates is not necessary for his road, but that if he lowered his rates in that section the Canadian Pacific management would probably retaliate in some other section. Now if the rates which we are paying in the mountains are not sufficiently high for the Canadian Pacific to make at least a fair profit on the business, I cannot for the life of me see why they should be so anxious to get as large a portion of that traffic as they are handling. Take the business, for instance, from northern Alberta. A survey of the situation will convince anybody that the Canadian National Railway should have practically all that traffic. The distance is much shorter, and the grade unquestionably is much better; but if you will look over the freight returns you will find that the Canadian Pacific are handling approximately about one-half of all the business that is going out that way. It is necessary to go down to Calgary and then west from there. Certainly they are getting an excessive freight rate, or they would not carry that freight over such a circuitous and extremely difficult grade as compared with the grade on the Canadian National. If we are going to have competition for lower rates, and that used to be the theory, that competition was the only way to lower them, we have the railroads now, we have the grade, and it seems to me that now is the time to enforce competition. If that is not done, by all manner of means let us quit trying to deceive ourselves and admit that competition is not a factor in railway rates. A few years ago, for instance, when our friends to the right here were in office, they undertook to lower ocean rates by using the merchant marine. The present government has altogether discarded that idea of using the merchant marine for lowering rates, and it is going to subsidize ships. As far as railroading goes, both these methods have been tried and neither has been found any good. So it seems to me, whether or not it is worth, while to discuss this question, that we must

have something different from what has already been tried, for both the methods tried up to date have failed. This whole question is one of outstanding importance, not to western Canada alone, but to the country at large.
At the time we discussed the Crowsnest pass agreement in 1922, the railroad companies put up a terrific howl about the amount of money they were going to lose if that agreement came into effect.	As we look over the
returns of the railroad companies since then, we find that their predictions have not come to pass at all. The railroad companies, especially in 1923, had a much better year than they had in 1922. Of course, it is only fair to state that we had an exceptionally heavy crop that year. But 1924, with a light crop, compared very favourably indeed with 1922. I do not care what question comes up for discussion, if it is of international importance at all, wheat will eventually be a factor in it, and if it is the desire of Canada to move wheat cheaply so that we can compete with other countries in the world, I do not think we can afford to ignore this mountain scale rate. I think it is also worth while to remember that wheat is not the only factor that enters into the situation. Alberta has practically an unlimited amount of coal. They also have considerable forests, and a good fur business. All these are materials which not only produce new wealth but which, if developed, will produce tonnage for our railroads.
When the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) was speaking to-night, he dwelt on one of the findings of the railway commission in which they said that in the prairie section, the long haul and the low cost of construction were some of the factors that should offset the lower rates in the east. That is only part of the situation. Certainly it must be much cheaper to get coal for the railroads in Alberta or anywhere in the mountains than in the eastern part of Canada, for it matters not where you have a depot in the west, there you have a coal mine practically beside it. Certainly it is much easier to get water for your engines in the mountains than it is in practically any part of the east. I have been told by engineers that you can get a better quality of water, water that works better in the engine and that gives no trouble in the boilers through corrosion, than you can in the east. I do not think anywhere through that mountain section they have any trouble with the engine boilers corroding. But that is not the case in the east. These are all matters which enter into the cost of railroad operation.
As far as railroad construction is concerned, I doubt if there is any part of Canada where
the road was built as cheaply in the first place, and was got into as good a condition so quickly as it was across the prairies.
In conclusion, I would ask the minister not only to give this matter his attention, but to try and get the ear of his colleagues in the government and try and do the fair thing by eliminating this mountain scale in its entirety.

I thank the minister for his statement, I think that is perfectly fair. I appreciate and to the full the complex nature of this problem. The question of freight rate structure is perhaps the most intricate problem in all the realm of economics. I know of nothing more intricate and nothing more complex, and I want to say further while we have this subject before us-that in my opinion, after fourteen years of intimate study as a layman of the problem, and after repeatedly bringing it to the attention of the House as I have for many years. I have come to the conclusion that this parliament, sitting as a body, can never expect to unravel and determine what is exactly the correct scale of freight rates to be charged in various parts of the country. I think it is an utterly hopeless task for a bod!y of this kind, but I do believe that a solution will be found only when the people of this country at large entertain in the railway commission, or some other body erected of that character, complete confidence and give to it the problem for its decision. Now, I apprehend this: That a large portion of the dissatisfaction through Canad'a arose, perhaps, four or five years ago because of an agitation against certain utterances of members of the railway board. I am not passing any judgment in the matter; the gentleman who was particularly charged with giving utterance to unfair or prejudiced views is now dead-I refer to the late Hon. Mr. Carvell. I am not for one moment joining in the hue and cry that went on in this country against the chairman of the railway commission, the late Mr. Carvell, but there is no doubt that that hue and cry, the attacks mad'e upon him-attacks made by men of very high standing within certain limits perhaps, such as the Minister of Agriculture-attacks that were made in many sections of the country against him, did undermine confidence in an institution that hitherto had held the unbounded confid'ence of the people of Canada at large, and from that time extreme difficulty has been ex-

perienced in connection with this question. You meet the public and suggest to them that the proper body to decide this technical subject is the railway board. The immediate reply is "We have no confidence in the railway board", and I recall, Sir, and I know other members of the House will recall, where, time after time, resolutions were passed by boards of trade, chambers of commerce, and various public bodies, expressing a lack of confidence in the railway board. This I think was the most unfortunate, the most disastrous thing that has happened in recent years in connection with the administration of affairs throughout the country. However, we have that condition.
At the same time we have a deep rooted conviction in the minds of a large section of the public that they have grievances. For instance, taking people in British Columbia, nothing in the world would persuade them that a grave injustice is not being done in connection with this mountain scale. They have a deep rooted conviction on the subject and, I may say, based upon very sound grounds. speechtext:
My hon. friend is unfortunately following a course that others have pursued; when a statement is produced- and I am producing such a statement- they try to put in my mouth a line of argument I am not seeking to make at all. I understand that undoubtedly the amount of the freight rate on an article ultimately affects the price of the article; but I want to point out that sometimes people attach a great deal of importance to and make almost a national issue of some secondary point as to the application of rates here and there, and wake up to find that no distinct advantage has accrued from it at all. That is all I was seeking to argue.
I want to impress upon the House that this whole problem is such a complicated one that it would be far better if this House could address itself to the necessity of restoring confidence in a body qualified to deal with the whole technical situation and direct that body. I believe absolutely in the railway board and without reserve in the railway board, and I think that we should restore confidence in it. If we have not confidence in that railway board, then we should erect a body in which we would have confidence and place this great problem of railway freight rates in their hands.
It is claimed and claimed correctly that the Railway Act is the guiding power, that is it controls and directs to a degree, and, shall I say, limits the power of the railway board. I realize that and I think perhaps this is the point that must be determined by this House; that in the Railway Act parliament declares that there shall be no unfair, unjust or unreasonable discrimination, and from these adjectives, these qualifying words, "unfair, unreasonable or unjust," arises a great deal of the trouble. Parliament is asked sometimes-indeed I recall a few years ago I asked parliament myself, by presenting a bill in this House-to declare that there shall be no discrimination at all. But I realize, after more complete study of the problem, that parliament could not fix it with safety in that form, because, if you fix the rate structure so that there will be absolutely no discrimination, you lead gradually into these schools of thought in regard to railway rates who hold to this, that the rate on a ton of silk should not be more than the rate on a ton of coal, because the weight carried on the railway is the same.
Mountain Freight Scale

For instance, to put it, perhaps, not in such an extreme manner, there are certain grades of ore high priced, or, let us say, carrying values of gold or copper that call for a higher rate than a low grade type of ore, and the argument is advanced sometimes: Why should this more valuable product which weighs exactly the same as regards a ton weight, as the less valuable ore, carry a higher rate of f>
eight? But these differences in classification must occur if we are going to function as a country at all, and everybody knows that. I do not know how many classifications there are. When you separate them into their atoms, they run into thousands, so that it is an utter impossibility for 'this House to determine exactly what rate shall be charged here or there or upon this or that article.
It might be claimed by some that my argument is against the resolution. It is not against the resolution. I stand behind this idea, that when a given arbitrary rate known as the mountain scale is shown to be inequitable and unfair, it should be removed, just as I say, in regard to other sections of Canada where it can be shown that a rate is unfair, then that rate should not be sustained. But I do not think it is the part of parliament to decide what is fair or is not fair in the question of rates. I do not want to be too critical of the government. This is not a motion in regard to which we can assume, as we often do, the role of a harsh critic of the government. I do not say this unkindly, but I am a little disappointed that the minister has not given to the House a somewhat fuller and more complete idea of the mind of the government in regard to this and kindred subjects. We have a somewhat nebulous suggestion in the Speech from the Throne that if we are good boys, we may expect at some time during the session an utterance by the government. I do not know of any better time than on this resolution. We are intensely interested and worried in British Columbia over this problem. I could go in*o detailed figures, but I do not wish to do so. Suffice it to say this: let us take, for instance, the movement of grain; the export rate on grain from the prairies to the coast is about double the same rate eastward. I cannot, for the life of me, see the justification for that, and these are things that are alarming, disturbing the people, that are worrying the people in business who are seeking to take advantage of natural and geographical situations. I know that the officers of the two great systems of railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Cana-d:an National, are intensely concerned over

this whole question of railway freight rates. It is unwise that we should drift along much longer without coming to some definite conclusion.
Before I sit down, let me repeat very briefly what I said a year ago with regard to this question. This structure that we call the freight rates tariff is the growth of probably half a century going through various phases of development, but I have discovered, in my study of the problem, that it has largely been directed and influenced by a desire on the part of those who have fixed the rates, to develop Canada. What was a good thing for the development of Canada, say twenty-five years ago, when the prairies were sparsely settled might not be an equitable or fair or proper thing to-day. Another point is this, that when our present system of freight-rate making was not inaugurated, but like Topsy, just grew, there was a distribution from the east westward and no distribution from the west eastward. With the construction and completion of the Panama canal in 1915, there was thrust, shall I say, into the whole problem an entirely new factor, in fact, an element that completely changed the principle upon which freight rates should be fixed. What do we find now? We have now the opportunity of distributing freight from two seaboards inward. What I want to suggest to this House is this: Whether we undertake a very detailed consideration of the problem or not, I believe this principle must be adopted in Canada for the fixation of freight rates, and that is the distribution of freight from the two seaboards inward. That, I think, is a basic, underlying, fundamental principle. If it is, there is no doubt that there will be vast, radical and almost revolutionary changes in some of the rates that are charged. But while I give utterance to this principle in, perhaps, a very general manner, I also realize that when I say there must be a revolutionary change in our freight rates structure, I am touching a very delicate and complicated question. It is a question too delicate and complex for this parliament to deal with. I hope I have made my position clear. If this resolution comes to a vote, I certainly am in favour of it as it stands, but I agree in a large measure with the minister that this whole question must be considered. For instance, I am faced with this possibility -and I want my hon. friend who proposes the resolution to recognize it-if you bring about a lowering in given rates, for example in British Columbia, we are at present enjoying certain other rates that are very much below that horizontal line to which we would like to bring these higher rates and it is only reasonable to expect that others will want to

Mountain Freight Scale
bring those lower rates up. I am not unreasonable; I cannot expect, if we are going to lower certain rates, that we are going to retain at the same time the lower and advantageous rates that we have on other commodities. So, while I do support the resolution in lowering or removing the mountain scale, I would like to put the rider on it that in doing that, we are not going to raise the commodity rates, for instance, on fruit, lumber, fish and some other commodities upon which wie enjoy very favourable and advantageous rates. That again injects into the consideration of this problem its very complexity and difficulty. I rose simply to declare my general position in connection with the proposal before the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been
listening, for the last few hours, to the views on freight rates expressed by our colleagues from the west. As it was so lucidly stated by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) there also exists a question of freight rates in the eastern provinces. Unfortunately, the members from the Maritime provinces are not here to-night, to air their grievances. However, the government is perfectly aware that the province of Quebec asks for a readjustment of freight rates. When the Prime Minister paid a visit to Quebec, about a month ago, at a banquet given in his honour, an hon. legislative councillor in proposing the health of the Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King) reminded him that there existed in a number of districts in our province, discrepancies of freight rates absolutely unjustifiable which had to be done away with as soon as possible. For instance, there is on the south shore below the Quebec bridge, two railways almost parallel: the old Intercolonial line which extends from the Maritime provinces to Montreal, and, further inland, at a distance of fifteen to twenty miles, the Transcontinental railway. These two lines are under the management of the Canadian National Railways.
What do we find on the sections of these two lines between New Brunswick and the Quebec bridge? Two railways in two different valleys.
The old Intercolonical railway which extends along the river as far as the Quebec bridge, has in a number of localities quite steep grades to climb and especially between Levis station and the Quebec bridge. There also exists quite a perceptible grade from the town of Montmagny on, in the direction of St. Charles, in the county of Bellechasse. There are practically no grades on the Transcontinental. Nevertheless what do we find? That the rates are much higher than those of the Intercolonial, and this for the same distance. Therefore, a discrimination exists which is to the disadvantage of the parishes occupying the centre of the counties of Tem-iscouata, Kamouraska, L'Islet, Montmagny, Bellechasse, Dorchester and Levis. Why this difference? It is evidently based upon a decision-probably fair-of the railway commission. This difference, however, should disappear at the same time as the high freight rates of the mountainous regions of British Columbia and Alberta.
Our farmers and settlers north of Quebec, along the Transcontinental, who have established themselves near the railway passing through Cochrane and Amos 'and reaching the Quebec bridge, a line which requires little traction, have also to suffer from freight rates that are not proportional to those of the railways which inn close to the shores of the St. Lawrence. Therefore, a discrimination exists which paralyzes the development of the northern part of the province of Quebec.
If we now cross to the other side of the river, this discrimination against the Transcontinental, in the five or six counties surrounding Levis, also hinders the development of a number of thriving parishes. It is impossible to open up the centre of Mont-magny, Bellechasse and L'Islet, if the freight rates are not lowered to the level of those given to our competitors along the Intercolonial railway, where these two lines are hardly fifteen miles apart. Why?
Should the government come to the conclusion that there exists sufficient ground to readjust the freight rates for the west, we, from the province of Quebec, ask to be as fairly dealt with.
Why two different rates for the same distance, on two parallel lines in the same counties?
We have noticed that, within the last years, under the plea of economy, some passenger trains had been discontinued on the Canadian National railways running through the counties on the south shore. The present service is so defective, so far as passenger and baggage are concerned, that it is almost impossible to travel. This is what, for instance, business men do wrho have to reach the parishes in the centre of these counties: They travel by the old Intercolonial line and hire cabs to bring them to the various places at which the Transcontinental stops.
We requested better service from the management of the National Railways, but without success, we were told that we had to practise economy.
Mountain Freight Scale

On the other hand we notice, in certain neighbouring provinces, that the passenger service is better than in the province of Quebec. However, it is very costly. The relative number of passengers carried by these trains from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or from Ontario is less than that of the province of Quebec. There are, Sir, two provinces which by themselves alone supply the greatest part of the country's traffic: the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. They supply almost forty per cent of all railway traffic.
We, from the province of Quebec, living on the south shore, if we consider the traffic service of the old Intercolonial or lines making up the Canadian National railway system, find that this part of the system from St. Rosalie to Campbellton brings in millions of dollars in profits, while there is a deficit in the service between Campbellton and Halifax. Shall we allow the spending in other provinces which have a better service than ours, of the profits realized in our own province?
I say there is a flaw in the service, and when the time comes to fully consider this question, when the time comes to submit our claims to the government, I can assure you that we, belonging to Quebec, shall have our eyes open. If rights and privileges are claimed, we shall equally request what we shall call rights or rather what will be mentioned throughout the country as privileges; but we do not think that, so far as we are concerned, one can call this privilege, because we dig down into our pockets so to maintain our lines, and, if we supply the freight, the least that we can expect is that this money be spent at home.
Now Sir, the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) who has just preceded me in this debate has hinted at a state of things which we are too often apt to forget. These gentlemen from British Columbia are at a disadvantage-I quite believe it-in some localities, in certain trades, owing to the existing high freight rates; but they have not admitted as frankly as the hon. member has just done that they have freight rates on certain items which are much below those we pay in the east.
Since the question of better readjusting the railway freight rates will soon be taken up, we shall insist on having these rates put on the same basis as those we pay in the east. It is all very well, Mr. Speaker, to talk of lowering the freight rates, it is all very well to say: We shall urge on the goverment our just claims, we shall endeavour to unite, province by province, section by section, so

as to assert certain rights however, we must not forget one thing which to me seems the most important part of the question of railway freight rates: if we further lower our railway rates, what problem shall we have to face? We shall be deprived of a few million dollars owing to the rates which this present resolution before the House demands, another few million dollars owing to the readjustment of rates in the west, a few millions in the north of Ontario, a few millions in the north of Quebec, perhaps some millions in the Maritime provinces,, a total, Sir, that we shall have to add to the already enormous deficits of the country's railways. Where shall we raise the money to meet these deficits? Borrow? All very well. Pay the interest? Shall we always borrow to meet the interest, or shall we impose taxes to meet the payments? We shall have to choose between these two methods.
On the other hand, we are asked to lower the taxes; everybody clamors for it. It is impossible to lower the taxes and the railway rates at the same time. We must either pay one way or the other. Should we be forced to lower our rates, we shall, on the other hand, be obliged to levy taxes.
There is no escape; the burden of taxation falls upon the consumer who eventually finds himself in such, a plight that he cannot make any further purchases, the wheels of commerce stop, and we shun Scylla to fall into Charybdis.
I think that the suggestion made by the hon. Minister of Railways should be adopted by the House. The discussion brought out, until now, the grievances and rights of our fellow citizens of British Columbia, Alberta and other western provinces; at this late hour, I humbly put before the House some of the problems which Quebec has to deal with in regard to this railway question, and if the hour was not so late, we would certainly hear from our friends and fellow citizens from the Maritime provinces. Would it not be more expedient, in view of this situation, not to further press the point, but to thoroughly consider the question and allow the government to add, perhaps, to this resolution the other questions which it might wish, in this connection, to submit to the House and to leave this question, for the moment, in abeyance. I agree with pleasure to the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Railways, and I think that the whole House will share these views, in order to ensure to the country more equitable railway rates, fairer to the west, but also to the east.

Mountain Freight Scale
Hon. R. J. MAiNION (Fort William and Rainy River):	So far as I am concerned,
this question of freight rates is too complicated for me to vote on a resolution of this kind. This matter has been argued and reargued in this country from coast to coast for many years now and we have had legal experts such as Mr. McGeer and Mr. Symington as well as railway experts from the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern Railways, all of whom have taken different attitudes both before the press of the country and the Board of Railway Commissioners. I am sure, therefore, that no ordinary member of parliament, like myself, and certainly no ordinary reader, could come to a decision on the justice of a question of this magnitude. If the resolution had merely stated that an unfair discrimination should be eliminated I should unhesitatingly support it. But I must point out that those who have taken part have naturally spoken from a sectional point of view; I do not intend this in any critical sense whatever, because in the very nature of things this is bound to be the case; but the fact is that those who have contributed to the debate have spoken from the standpoint of their own sections. Now, if I spoke from the standpoint of my section I should probably oppose the resolution; and that I do not wish to do. If the-resolution were adopted and its principle put into effect it would probably injure the part of the country which I represent. I do not intend to explain that point because I am sure that it will be appreciated by those who understand the freight rate question as it affects the west. But what I say is true, nevertheless. I do not choose, however, to oppose the motion. Whatever I might do on any other question, I have no desire to take any stand in this matter which might be injurious to the rest of the country although helpful to my own district, and I flatter myself that my constituents are big enough to view a question like this from the point of view of the welfare of the whole country. At the same time I do not feel capable of deciding by my vote a matter that is so complicated. There is in this country a body which, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has pointed out, should be the proper judicial authority to settle any matter of this kind, and that is the Board of Railway Commissioners. And I agree with him that if that body has not the confidence of the Canadian people then we should certainly either endeavour to restore the public confidence in the board or get a board constituted in whom the people will trust. If there is anyone in this House who should know the question a
little better than anybody else, it would be a member of the government.

speechtext:
The resolution introduced by my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) is a phase of probably one of the most intricate questions with which this parliament will have to deal this session. As a representative from the province of British Columbia, it is not necessary for me to state that I am thoroughly alive to and know something about the handicap under which that province has suffered during the past and at the present time. But knowing the condition as I do, and' knowing the efforts that have recently been made by the people of British Columbia through the government of that province, who have employed trained counsel and made an exhaustive study of the question, extending over a period of years, and who have appeared before the tribunal which was considered the proper authority in matters of this kind-and created by the Parliament of Canada-I would hesitate to-night in disposing of this matter summarily. In fact, I should be very much perturbed if that were done. I am absolutely satisfied of the sincerity of the hon. gentleman who has submitted the resolution. He fives on the border
Mountain Freight Scale

of British Columbia ana' this question affects the province of Alberta almost as greatly as it does my own province, and I believe entirely in the hon. gentleman's sincerity and in the genuineness of his motive in bringing forward the matter. But I would ask him whether he thinks it wise to allow the question to go to a vote on the evidence that has been submitted this evening or on such evidence as might be brought forward! tonight during this debate, even if it went into the hours of the morning. I do not believe we are qualified to dispose of the question on the evidence we have. As a matter of fact, from my own information on the subject, it seems to me that it is only by the most ^ complete and exhaustive study of the question that one .would be (capable of coming to a sound judgment on the question. After the appearance of counsel for British Columbia before the railway commission some two years ago, there was an appeal from the commission and this question was argued before the Privy Council, the argument extending over two or three days. I listened1 to it with the greatest interest and fully realized the intricacy and difficulty of the question. As I have said, the resolution of my hon. friend deals only (with one phase of a great problem which is to be dealt with by parliament; in other words, it is anticipating action which is foreshadowed in the Speech from the Throne. Let me quote from that document.
It is the opinion of my advisers that the attention of parliament at the present session should be directed more particularly to the desirability of effecting freer movement of commodities through an equalization of railway freight rates as between provinces and localities and through a lowering of carrying charges upon shipments by water.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: Will the hon. minister tell us what the government intends that to mean?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
Well, I think we will have to "wait and see", as we say nowadays. That is what I am trying to advise my hon. friend from West Edmonton. Rather than jeopardize a good case, which I believe will appeal to the members of this House and to the people of the Dominion, I think it would be wise to allow it to stand until the whole question of freight rates can be brought before parliament. Then in the course of debate the case can be again brought forward to see if the government cannot suggest ways and1 means whereby it may be properly dealt with at this session. There can be no question of my entire confidence in the case that the province of British Columbia has made, but as a member from that province who has followed the question with great 
interest, I think it would be inadvisable for parliament to take action this evening, and in view of my remarks, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: I have no right to speak on the motion, but I had intended to express my views before the minister moved the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the
House that the hon. gentleman shall have leave to withdraw 'his motion?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I have to say in the way. of a general enunciation of views on this subject I have already stated m this House on more than one occasion. It is this, that following the erection of the railway commission and the delegation to it of defined powers, the function of parliament is only to declare the principles upon which that commission shall act and which it shall apply to all the varied schedules of railway rates and all the varied phases of that complex question. The Railway Act now embodies the principles which parliament in its wisdom up to the present time has thought fit to pass to the commission and to declare its faith in. The government appears to be of the view that some new principles must be enunciated. What they are it does not for the life of it 'know. Consequently it resorts in the Speech from the Throne to language which means nothing whatever. For the first two sessions the Speech from the Throne rang the changes on co-ordination and co-operation. Those vanished into thin air; they became so grating to the ear that last session was substituted the word "equalization." It was applied in two or three ways in the Speech from the Throne a year ago, notably to flour; there was to be equalization of the rates on flour. What that meant no one in the House was advised, and finally by effluxion of time we learned that it meant nothing whatever. We are now told that there is to be equalization of freight rates as between provinces and localities. I .asked the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) what the government had in mind in that sentence. He declines to tell us. I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King)-he who asserts that he is thoroughly convinced of the merits of the case of British Columbia, but who does not like to declare he is convinced in this resolution-I asked him what was in the mind of

Mountain Freight Scale
the government in that phrase, and from the question be backs gallantly away. The only conclusion is that the government had nothing in mind at all. Their object in putting the phrase in the Speech from the Throne was to convince hon. gentlemen who were deeply interested that the government had the subject under attention and hoped some time to declare something specifically to this House.
Now, if it is a fact that our duty is to impress into legislation the principles upon which the rate structure itself must be framed by the railway commission, then such a resolution as this has no place here at all. This is a matter of the application of a principle. Undoubtedly no one desires British Columbia to suffer under any unjust disability, under any discrimination taken in the whole; but it is a question whether or not you can remove a certain mountain scale of rates and at the same time leave all the rest of the rates and not discriminate in favour of the province. Consequently it is for the railway commission-a body of experts-to find whether or not there can be fairness, equality, to all the provinces, and this resolution put into effect. For that reason I am in favour of the adjournment of the debate, I am in favour of this matter going to the railway commission. If the government wants to declare some new principles, let it come down with its policy and we will act upon that policy; but my own opinion is this,-and while it is pretty close to the event one should not perhaps venture a prophecy-I venture to think that after we get this new declaration of principles we will find it is just a prolonged circumlocution, a mass of verbiage, resulting in a merely circuitous repetition of the principles that are in the Railway Act to-day. I fancy that after the whole thing is down we will find it is just a restatement in language akin to that so often employed in recent Speeches from the Throne-a restatement of the law as it is now.
Why is it, though, that we have these resolutions? Is it not just because this government has invited them by its own course?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: Are they new to this government?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
Pretty new. I have never followed any of them, in power or in opposition. I do not recall being bothered with them before. This government, by attacks on the railway commission in opposition, has undermined confidence in it, and none is more guilty than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who sits now with his head
down and does not like this discussion; none is more guilty than he. They have undermined confidence in the commission; they have encouraged agitation against it; they have encouraged an agitation to throw into the maelstrom of parliament a task parliament is unfit to perform. Two sessions ago, in order to gain the favour of hon. gentlemen to my left, they took a course they knew was based on no sound principle at all. They undertook to declare for a policy of restoration of a certain definite scale of rates which has landed this country in chaos, which to-day has us in a position from which we can scarcely escape. All this they did in order simply to maintain a majority in parliament and themselves in the sweets of power. From this they must escape. When they took this course I told them these things would come upon them, that if they answered to the demand of the prairies for a certain definite scale they would have to answer the demand of the Maritime provinces, and has not that demand arisen? Is it not ringing through the Maritime provinces now? Has it not been ringing in the ears of the government every month since? And they cannot answer it. Now they are called on by British Columbia to step in and do the work the railway commission should have done, and should have done with the confidence of the Canadian people. They could expect nothing else. All last summer the Prime Minister of Canada went on the stump throughout the west and declared the policy of his government was to restore the Crowsnest pass rates, and behold! he says, we have done it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
If that is the policy of
the government, it is the policy of the government to answer this resolution now, and to say yes or no. If it is the duty of the government to restore specific rates to one part of the country, it is its duty to say yes or no to this resolution, and not to hide behind the commission. The fact of the matter is the government took the course dictated by political expediency for the moment, and to-night it is paying the penalty. A government cannot stand to that course. It 'has to reverse itself. Whatever the humiliation may be, whatever the contortions may be, that reversion is going to take place this session.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
I
wish to say a word or two before this resolution is finally dealt with. I am heartily in favour of the principle of the resolution.
Mountain Freight Scale

The people of British Columbia have been suffering for many years, and are suffering yet, from the mountain scale, which we feel is an injustice to-day west of the mountains. At the time of the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, owing to the extra cost of construction through the Rocky and Selkirk mountains, large subsidies were granted to the company to offset the extra cost; and when they began to operate their lines, to offset the extra cost of transportation between the prairie and the coast, this mountain scale was allowed. At that time the volume of freight and passenger traffic was very small, but since then it has increased very materially. Since that time, too, something more important has happened; that is, we have had a railway constructed through the Yellow-head pass, where the grade is very much better than it is on the Canadian Pacific. I 'have been informed by engineers that we have a better grade from Edmonton to Vancouver than is to be found from Edmonton all the way to Fort William; that is, the grade through the Yellowhead pass at the highest point between Vancouver and Edmonton is lower than the grade from Edmonton to Fort William at its highest point, indicating that they can handle their trains through the Yellowhead pass a.t a very reasonable cost indeed. But has it had any effect? No. The mountain rate still prevails, based on the cost of operating over the Canadian Pacific railway, .and that is why British Columbians feel to-day that an injustice is being done to them.
There is one other point I feel is more important than this mere matter of trade in British Columbia, and that is that we have, lying west of the Great Lakes, one of the largest areas of agricultural land in the whole of Canada. Much of that territory can ship with a profit by way of Vancouver. I think we can all agree on this principle: that if we are going to be able to compete in the markets of the world with our agricultural and other products, we must have as easy access as possible to tidewater, and we must be able to ship these products at the very lowest possible rate. I do not propose to take up any more time except to say that I endorse the principle of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy).

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make my position clear in regard to this resolution, as it involves a very important question for British Columbia.
I do not wish to be accused of giving silent

assent in any way to the position taken by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) on this resolution. This question of the elimination of the mountain rate is a very important one for British Columbia, (but I would like to point out to the House that it is not the whole question as it affects freight rates for British Columbia. I have the honour to represent the southeastern district of the province of British Columbia. We are agreed upon the principle of the elimination, to some extent, of the mountain freight rate scale where there is discrimination, but the people of the West Kootenay district are also interested in another freight rate problem. They have their own local problems, and if this resolution came to a vote I would be compelled, under the circumstances, to vote against it. I have always believed that it is impossible for parliament either to tear down or build up a freight rate structure. In my opinion this is a question to be referred to some tribunal which is in a positron either to eliminate or build up a freght rate structure. I cannot vote for this resolution because I do not know what the consequences would be so far as the southeastern pan of British Columbia is concerned; I do not know what the effects would be regarding ether parts of British Columbia. I want to dc what is fair and right by my province, and I must also keep in mind particularly the views of my own district. I feel that by voting for this resolution I should be giving practically a blanket vote for the elimination of the mountain freight rates without knowing what the consequences would be to my own district and to other parts of the Dominion. Therefore I cannot support the resolution as it stands.

Is the House ready for
the question?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
I think the House will
agree, in view of the importance of the issues involved in the resolution moved by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) that further consideration of those issues should be had. The House is asked to express an opinion that the scale of freight rates in force in the mountain section of British Columbia should be abolished. Hon. gentlemen from every other part of the country, who are interested in the question of a proper adjustment of freight rates, must realize that this matter cannot be dealt with piecemeal- that it would be very imprudent for this House to express an opinion as to what should be the freight rates in one particular part of the country without taking into considers-

Miners and Steel Workers
tion the whole problem of the earnings of the railways. This is the greatest problem which confronts this House and it has been, I do not hesitate to say from my long parliamentary experience, the greatest problem that has confronted the Canadian people in the last quarter of a century. Now it is very well understood there is before the Supreme Court of Canada, and no doubt a decision will be rendered in a very short time, the question as to whether or not what is known as the Crowsnest pass rates are in force to-day. Upon the effect of that decision will depend very largely the conclusion to which this House or the railway commission may come as to what ought to be the rates in any part of Canada, and I think the House will agree with me that it is the part of wisdom for us to await that decision before we attempt, so far as the House is concerned, to express any opinion as to how this question should be dealt with. I therefore, Mr. Speaker, beg to move the adjournment of the debate, so that before the matter comes up again, or before the government deals with the question in a general way, we may have the advantage of further information.

Motion agreed to.
